chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Isḥāq al-Aḥmar from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥammād from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, who said:

A man came to Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) to collect his debt from him. He said, 'We do not have anything with us today, but a shipment (khiṭr) and a mark/brand of goods (wasimah) will come to us, so they will be sold and we will give you [the money], if God wills.' The man said to him, 'Promise me [a specific time/commitment].' He said, 'How can I promise you when I am more hopeful about what I do not hope for [certainty] than I am about what I do hope for [uncertainty].'

key_terms.وَسِمَةٌ: a marked or branded item / goods identified by a mark
key_terms.يَقْتَضِيهِ: to collect a debt / demand payment

ai.seo_question: How did the Imams handle debt collection and financial obligations according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Imam’s pragmatic approach to debt settlement, distinguishing between immediate liquidity and future assets (such as goods or livestock). The rhetorical paradox—'I hope for what I do not expect more than I hope for what I expect'—highlights the theological nuance between *rajāʾ* (hope in divine facilitation) and *yaqīn* (certainty of outcome), reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on maintaining trust (*amāna*) even when exact timing is uncertain. It serves as a model for creditors to accept conditional promises grounded in sincere intent rather than rigid guarantees.
